description: We are the Goofy Goobers! Let's have F.U.N. together :)
summary: What happens to a place when an AI data center moves in—and what could happen next? Footprint Atlas turns NASA Earth observations into an interactive 3D environmental investigation that students, residents and decision-makers can understand. Explore five study sites in Memphis, Ashburn, Abilene and The Dalles; move through time; and compare air pollution, vegetation and surface heat with the surrounding region. Clear maps, charts and numerical comparisons show what changed, where, by how much and whether the trend is statistically significant. Water-use evidence and regional climate scenarios add context. Supported trend extensions through 2035 and NASA climate scenarios to 2100 are clearly separated from historical observations. A low-poly landscape connects the measurements to recognizable neighborhoods. Our goal is to make the environmental footprint of digital infrastructure easier to investigate, while showing uncertainty, missing evidence and the limits of what satellite data can tell us. Changes near a facility are not automatically caused by it.
details:
Footprint Atlas — Mapping the environmental footprint of our digital world.

THE QUESTION

What happens to the environment when an AI data center moves in, and what could happen next? Data centers are expanding quickly, but the changes around them are hard for the public to investigate. Footprint Atlas gives students, communities, researchers, planners and developers a shared way to explore the evidence.

EXPLORE A PLACE, THEN FOLLOW THE EVIDENCE

Our browser-based 3D globe opens five prepared study areas: xAI Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 in Memphis, Data Center Alley in Ashburn, Stargate Abilene, and Google The Dalles. A timeline, before/after comparisons, readable values and charts connect NASA measurements to places people recognize. Users can switch between surface heat, vegetation greenness, nitrogen dioxide, aerosol haze and regional air temperature, with water-related layers and sourced facility water-use context. Low-poly neighborhoods, mapped streets and buildings, vegetation, wind trails and moving activity make the landscape approachable. Visual activity and procedural scenery are illustrative; the measurements and model outputs remain separately identified.

HOW WE ADDRESS THE CHALLENGE

The challenge asks what is changing, where, by how much, and whether it is statistically significant. We compare each study area with a surrounding reference ring, account for seasonal patterns, calculate Sen’s slope and confidence intervals, and use Mann–Kendall/seasonal trend tests with autocorrelation safeguards. Before/after comparisons help identify timing; nearby-region comparisons help distinguish local patterns from broader change. Source, unit, time coverage and missing-data information accompany the evidence. Statistical calculations are checked against SciPy reference results.

NASA DATA AT THE CORE

NASA GIBS supplies MODIS daytime/nighttime land-surface temperature, NDVI greenness and aerosol optical depth; Aura OMI and Sentinel-5P TROPOMI provide NO₂ context. HLS gives higher-resolution imagery, OPERA highlights land disturbance, and MERRA-2 and GLDAS supply regional temperature, precipitation and soil-moisture context. NASA POWER provides weather history. GEOS-FP analysed winds drive the wind display and conditional dispersion screening. NASA CMR supports imagery discovery. Giovanni/Harmony acquisition workflows are included, with incomplete imported histories identified rather than presented as available measurements.

LOOKING AHEAD WITHOUT HIDING UNCERTAINTY

Supported statistical trend extensions run through 2035 and mean “if the historical trend continues.” Per-pixel extensions for heat, greenness, NO₂ and haze are filtered by evidence quality and significance. Separately, NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 provides regional climate scenarios through 2100 using five climate models and SSP2-4.5/SSP5-8.5. These explore regional temperature, extreme heat and rainfall; they do not predict an individual data center’s future footprint. Historical observations, trend extensions and climate scenarios are labelled separately. Conditional Gaussian-plume screening uses wind and sourced inputs; without verified emissions, it represents relative dilution rather than a measured air concentration.

WHAT THE ANALYSIS CAN SHOW

The current analysis finds a regional warming signal around Ashburn and additional nighttime surface warming relative to its surroundings. It also identifies greenness changes at the Memphis sites. Other signals are weaker: the Colossus 1 NO₂ before/after comparison is borderline rather than statistically significant at the 0.05 level, and the project does not find a significant aerosol-haze increase across the study sites. Showing weak or absent evidence is part of the investigation, not a reason to invent an effect.

WHY THIS IS USEFUL

The creative contribution is connecting Earth observations, transparent statistics, numerical explanations and a navigable 3D landscape in one investigation. A learner can locate a facility, rewind the timeline, inspect a change, compare it with the surrounding region, then explore a clearly labelled future scenario. The intended impact is better public understanding and more informed questions about digital infrastructure and environmental change.

TOOLS AND IMPLEMENTATION

The live web app uses JavaScript/HTML/CSS, CesiumJS and Chart.js. Python handles data acquisition, geospatial processing, statistical analysis and scenario products; a Node.js/TypeScript job API connects supported model jobs to the web experience. Prepared products support the static deployment; on-demand jobs require the backend service. OpenStreetMap, Copernicus elevation, Esri imagery, USGS observations, public inventories and utility records add geographic and local context. The project includes original procedural low-poly models and credited Poly Haven sky photography. Unreal Engine/Cesium for Unreal support a separate cinematic demonstration.

BOUNDARIES AND NEXT STEPS

Satellite pixels can cover more than the facility, NO₂ columns are not ground-level exposure, and surface temperature is not the same as air temperature. A change near a data center does not establish causation; weather, urban growth, land clearing and other sources can contribute. We do not claim a calibrated groundwater/watershed balance, future water-quality forecast, crop-yield forecast or validated noise model. Coverage and import gaps remain visible. There is no trained machine-learning forecasting model: future views use established statistics and published climate simulations.

AI ASSISTANCE AND ATTRIBUTION

AI coding assistance, including OpenAI Codex, supported implementation, debugging, testing, research organization, interface design and documentation. Scientific observations come from the cited providers; statistical outputs and published climate scenarios are not LLM-generated measurements. Project text was also prepared with AI assistance and checked against the repository and presentation.

TRY IT AND INSPECT THE METHODS
